concept_panel.title: System Design Requirements
concept_panel.explanation: System design starts by clarifying what the system must do and what qualities it must have. Functional requirements describe behavior; non-functional requirements describe scale, latency, availability, durability, privacy, and cost constraints. Good designs tie APIs and data models to access patterns. Jumping to tools before requirements usually produces weak answers.
key_takeaways: Clarify functional requirements first.
Non-functional requirements drive architecture.
Access patterns shape APIs and data models.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can turn vague product goals into concrete engineering constraints.
concept_panel.practical_example: A feed service design changes depending on read/write ratio, freshness needs, and fan-out size.

concept_panel.title: Caching
concept_panel.explanation: A cache stores previously computed or fetched data so repeated reads avoid expensive work. Caching improves latency and reduces load, but introduces staleness and invalidation problems. You should cache data that is read often, expensive to compute, and safe to serve slightly stale. Always explain cache hit, cache miss, TTL, and invalidation.
key_takeaways: Cache hits avoid database or service work.
Cache misses still need the source of truth.
Invalidation and staleness are the main trade-offs.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand performance trade-offs and stale-data risk.
concept_panel.practical_example: A product catalog can be cached in Redis with a TTL if updates are infrequent.

questions.prompt: Writes arrive in bursts, and users do not need immediate processing. Which component helps?
questions.explanation: Queues absorb bursts and decouple producers from workers, at the cost of delayed processing.

concept_panel.title: Queues and Backpressure
concept_panel.explanation: A queue decouples producers from workers. It smooths bursts by storing work until consumers can process it, which improves resilience but adds delay. Queues are useful when immediate completion is not required. The design must handle retries, duplicates, dead-letter queues, and visibility into lag.
key_takeaways: Queues smooth bursty writes.
Async processing trades immediacy for resilience.
Consumer lag and duplicate handling matter.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand async system design and backpressure.
concept_panel.practical_example: Send email jobs to a queue so signup responses do not wait for the email provider.

concept_panel.title: Replication and Replica Lag
concept_panel.explanation: Replication copies data from a primary or leader to follower replicas. It can improve read capacity and availability, but followers may lag behind recent writes. A user who writes to the leader and immediately reads from a lagging replica may see stale data. The design must decide which reads require freshness.
key_takeaways: Replicas help read scale and availability.
Replica lag creates stale-read risk.
Read-your-writes may require leader reads or session-aware routing.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand consistency trade-offs in replicated systems.
concept_panel.practical_example: After updating a profile, route that user's next profile read to the leader until replicas catch up.

questions.prompt: A username must be unique globally during failover. What should you prioritize?
questions.explanation: Uniqueness is an invariant. Protect it with a strongly consistent path even if other parts can be eventually consistent.
options: Strong consistency for the uniqueness check
questions.answer: Strong consistency for the uniqueness check

concept_panel.title: Consistency vs Availability
concept_panel.explanation: Consistency describes what reads are allowed to observe after writes. Some invariants, like unique usernames or bank balances, need strong consistency. Other values, like social counters, can often be eventually consistent. During failures, stronger consistency may reduce availability because coordination is required.
key_takeaways: Use strong consistency for hard invariants.
Eventual consistency can fit counters and feeds.
Consistency choices trade off with latency and availability.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can choose guarantees based on business invariants.
concept_panel.practical_example: A like count can lag briefly, but a payment ledger should not accept conflicting balances.

questions.prompt: A like counter can be stale for a few seconds. Which trade-off is acceptable?
questions.explanation: Counters and feeds often tolerate temporary staleness, which can reduce coordination and improve availability.

questions.prompt: A design stores all tenants in one partition by tenant_type, and enterprise traffic overloads one node. What failed?
questions.explanation: Partition keys need enough cardinality and balanced traffic. Skewed keys create hot partitions.

concept_panel.title: Sharding and Hot Partitions
concept_panel.explanation: Sharding splits data across nodes so one machine does not hold all data or write load. The shard key decides where each record goes. A poor key can concentrate traffic on one shard and create a hot partition. Sharding increases capacity but makes routing, rebalancing, and cross-shard operations harder.
key_takeaways: Sharding partitions data across nodes.
Shard-key choice controls balance.
Skew creates hot shards and operational pain.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand horizontal scaling and data distribution failures.
concept_panel.practical_example: Partitioning by tenant_type can overload the enterprise shard if enterprise tenants dominate traffic.

coding_challenges.instructions: Implement classify_status_code(code: int) -> str. Return success for 200-299, redirect for 300-399, client_error for 400-499, server_error for 500-599, and unknown otherwise.
